outcomes: Draws the square for a lone passed pawn and says whether the king catches it when it is his move and when it is the pawn's move
Names two ways the square rule misleads: your own king's help and a pawn on its second rank

steps.text: Can a lone king catch a runaway pawn? Count the pawn's steps to the eighth rank (for a black pawn, count towards the first rank) and draw a square with that many squares on a side, starting at the pawn. If the defending king is inside the square, or steps into it on his move, he catches the pawn. This **rule of the square** is a heuristic: it counts only the pawn and the defending king.

steps.caption: Black to move. His king cannot get into the pawn's square in time.

line.say: Black's king heads for the pawn's path.
The pawn steps forward and the square shrinks.
Black's king takes another step towards the pawn.
Black's king is still a step too far.
The pawn reaches the seventh rank.
Black's king reaches d7, one file too far to touch b8.

claims.statement: With Black to move, Black loses.

steps.text: **The square rule has limits.** (1) Your own king can escort the pawn, so a king inside the square may still lose. (2) A pawn on its second rank can move two squares, so draw the square from the square it will reach after the double step. Both are limits of a rule of thumb: the square counts only the pawn and the defending king, so check the position before you trust it.
